uncited: **Eye Position:** The 3D origin of the eye ($E_L$ for left, $E_R$ for right).
**View Direction:** The vector pointing from the eye to the focal point.
**Projection Parameters:** Field of view (FOV), aspect ratio, and near/far clipping planes.
**Calculate Eye Positions:** Determine the left and right eye positions based on the central camera position and the IPD.
The eyes are typically offset horizontally from the center.
**Define Frustums:** Construct two perspective projection matrices (or view frustums).
*   For symmetric stereo, the frustums are symmetric around their respective optical axes.
*   For off-axis stereo, the frustums are non-symmetric to ensure the projection planes coincide [S2, unofficial].
**Transform Geometry:** Transform all 3D scene vertices into the clip space of the left eye frustum.
**Render Left Image:** Rasterize the transformed geometry to produce the left eye image.
**Transform Geometry:** Transform all 3D scene vertices into the clip space of the right eye frustum.
**Render Right Image:** Rasterize the transformed geometry to produce the right eye image.
Let $C$ be the center of the screen or focal point.
Let $IPD$ be the interpupillary distance.
The left eye position $E_L$ and right eye position $E_R$ are derived from the camera center.
The projection matrix $P$ for each eye is calculated using the standard perspective projection formula, adjusted for the specific eye's position and orientation.
*   **Convergence Distance:** The distance at which the left and right view directions intersect.
*   **Vertical Parallax:** If the projection planes of the left and right eyes do not coincide, vertical parallax occurs, causing visual discomfort.
This is mitigated by using off-axis projection or careful alignment [S2, unofficial].
*   **Clipping:** Geometry may be clipped differently by the two frustums, potentially causing popping artifacts if not handled carefully.
*   **Time Complexity:** Double the rendering time of a single perspective view, as two full passes are required.
*   **Memory Complexity:** Requires storage for two image buffers (or one interleaved buffer).
Vertical parallax can cause discomfort if not managed.
*   **When to Use:** When stereoscopic depth is required for visualization or interaction.
*   **When Not to Use:** When hardware support is unavailable or when performance is critical and depth is not necessary.
Stereo projection is a fundamental technique in computer graphics for creating stereoscopic 3D images.
It is based on the principle of binocular vision, where each eye sees a slightly different perspective of the world.
The technique is widely used in virtual reality, 3D movies, and scientific visualization.
